'''Cupeño''', or '''Pá{{hamza}}anexily''', is an [[Uto-Aztecan languages|Uto-Aztecan]] language that was spoken by the [[Cupeño people]] of southern [[California]], United States.<ref name="KPBS">{{cite news |last1=Corelis |first1=Carolyne |title=The little radio station that's keeping Indigenous culture alive on the air |url=https://www.kpbs.org/news/arts-culture/2025/06/17/keeping-indigenous-culture-alive-on-the-air |access-date=14 November 2025 |agency=KPBS |date=June 17, 2025}}</ref> [[Roscinda Nolásquez]] was the last native speaker of Cupeño.<ref name="hill2005grammar">{{Cite book
| publisher = University of California Press
| volume = 136
| url = http://escholarship.org/uc/item/2mz6t67j
| last = Hill
| first = Jane H.
| title = A Grammar of Cupeño
| series = UC Publications in Linguistics
| date = 2005-10-18
}}</ref> The Cupeño people now speak English. The native name {{lang|cup|Kupangaxwicham}} means 'people from the sleeping place', referring to their traditional homeland, prior to 1902, of Ktipa (at the base of [[Warner Springs, California |Warner's Hot Springs]]).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Sturtevant |first=William C. |title=Handbook of North American Indians |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |year=1978 |volume=8 |location=California}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Did you know Cupeño is awakening? |url=http://www.endangeredlanguages.com/lang/2009 |access-date=2022-07-11 |website=Endangered Languages |language=en}}</ref> A smaller village was located to the south of Ktipa, named [[Wildkalpa]]. 

Throughout the 1890s, there was debate over whether the Cupeño people should be allowed to continue living on traditional Cupeño territory.<ref name=":0" /> After many years of public protests, the [[Supreme Court of California|California Supreme Court]] decided to relocate the Cupeño people to the [[Pala Indian Reservation|Pala Reservation]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />{{when|date=January 2023}}

Cupeño shows linguistic influence from both the languages that preceded it and the [[Yuman–Cochimí languages|Yuman]]-speaking [[Kumeyaay|Ipai]], who share their southern border.<ref name=":0" />

==Geographic distribution==
The language was originally spoken in Cupa, Wilaqalpa, and Paluqla, located in [[San Diego County, California|San Diego County]], California, and later around the [[Pala Indian Reservation]].

{{IPA|/ɛ/}} and {{IPA|/o/}} primarily occur in Spanish [[loanwords]] but also serve as [[allophony|allophones]] of {{IPA|/ə/}} in native Cupeño words.

{{IPA|/i/}} can be realized as {{IPAblink|ɪ}} in closed syllables and as {{IPAblink|e}} in some open syllables.

{{IPA|/u/}} may reduce to a schwa in unstressed syllables.

{{IPA|/ə/}} also appears as {{IPAblink|ɨː}} when long and stressed, {{IPAblink|o}} after labials and {{IPA|[q]}}, and as {{IPAblink|ɛ}} before {{IPA|[w]}}.

{{IPA|/a/}} is also realized as {{IPAblink|ɑ}} before uvulars.<ref name="hill2005grammar" />

== Morphology ==
Cupeño is an [[agglutinative]] language, where words use suffix complexes for a variety of purposes with several [[morpheme]]s strung together. It is dominantly [[Head-directionality parameter|head-final]], with a mostly strict word order ([[Subject–object–verb word order|SOV]])<ref name="hill2005grammar" /> for some constituents, such as genitive-noun constructions. However, in certain contexts, there is flexibility in the word order, allowing verbs to be shifted to the initial part of a sentence or arguments to follow verbs.<ref name="hill2005grammar" />

=== Nouns ===
Nouns, as well as demonstratives, determiners, quantifiers, and adjectives, in Cupeño are marked for case and number and agree with each other in complex nominal constructions.<ref name="hill2005grammar" />

=== Verbs ===
Cupeño inflects its verbs for [[transitivity (grammar)|transitivity]], [[Grammatical tense|tense]], [[Grammatical aspect|aspect]], [[Grammatical mood|mood]], person, number, and [[evidentiality]].

Evidentiality in Cupeño is expressed with [[clitics]], typically appearing near the beginning of the sentence:

''={{lang|cup|kuʼut}}'' 'reportative' (''{{lang|cup|mu}}={{lang|cup|kuʼut}}'' 'and it is said that...')
''={{lang|cup|am}}'' 'mirative' 
''={{lang|cup|$he}}'' 'dubitative'

There are two inflected moods, realis ''={{lang|cup|pe}}'' and irrealis ''={{lang|cup|eʼp}}''.
